utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Are the interpreters here? Yes. I am glad that you are still well and kicking. Good morning to the Prosecution and the Defence, Mr. Krstic, the Court reporters, and the witness, who is here too. Good morning. Have you had a good rest, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And are you feeling well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to resume our hearing with your testimony, and it is Mr. McCloskey who is going to continue with the questions. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness L, yesterday we left off where you came to the execution area with a small group of fellow Muslim men and were shot down and you were lying in the field listening to things. Can you tell us, as you lay there after your fellows had been shot, what you heard happening around you as the time went on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the men had been killed, I heard a group getting together who called each other by name, and they were talking. I then recognised one of them called Gojko Simic, who used to work with me in the same company for at least 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about that. You say you saw -- or you say, excuse me, you heard men speaking. Were those -- how do you know they weren't Muslim men that had survived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because they called each other by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what names did you hear them call each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Gojko, Vojo, Risto, and they called another one by nickname, but I haven't remembered that nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long did you have a chance to hear these men speaking to each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to hear the voice of the person -- of the various people clearly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard this one in particular, the one I knew. He said that he should kiss those of us who had been killed because he thought we were all dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to recognise Gojko's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I knew him for many years, and his voice was typical. He didn't have a very clear way of expressing himself. There was a lisp in his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you know him from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him because we worked in the same company and we also come from the same municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from, what village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Orahovac, Zvornik municipality, and Grbovci and Orahovac belong to the same local community, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know how many years ago you worked with him in the company in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from 1977 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your connection with him at the company? Were you equal workers or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were both of the same occupation. We never argued. We were always on good terms with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you friends? Did you see each other socially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. We were acquaintances at work, but we never visited one another, because we lived quite a way away from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was the last time you had actually seen him before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, on the 3rd of April, when I left Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you describe Gojko Simic for us? What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Simic was rather like me by height, perhaps a little lower. He had more hair than me. He had two golden teeth. He was fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit 100? And could we put it on the ELMO so we can point it out?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is a protected witness, so there could be a problem if you place the photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The people in the photographs are not protected, but thank you for your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me ask you the question. Can you -- I've shown you this photograph within the last day or two and asked you to point out Gojko Simic. Were you able to do that when I asked you to do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, could you point out the person that you recognise as Gojko Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, that was the middle person in the bottom row. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And prior to hearing the soldiers speaking, referring to themselves -- or referring to each other as Gojko, Vojo, and Risto, did you hear the sounds of any equipment or anything besides the trucks that were dropping off victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the left there was a dredger, we used to call it, excavating machine, that was digging a hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as you're listening to Gojko and the others talk, could you get an idea of how many were in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my judgement, because three of them were left behind when they went off to another place to kill some more, there were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what else you heard this small group of soldiers talking about as you were lying nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they got together, close to this earth-moving machine, all of them wanted to go to the meadow to kill people. That is what they said. Then the person driving the machine said, "If you turn off the machine, I will go with you. I don't want to go on working." And then Gojko Simic said, "Collect your ammunition and let's go to the meadow to kill the men," the meadow from which the hay had been collected. When he left, three Serb soldiers stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, were you able to see any of this, or were you just hearing this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only discern them in the dark. I couldn't really see them, it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind that the voice you heard was that of Gojko Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt in my mind. I am 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell from the discussions that you heard who was in charge of this small group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what he said, the order was to collect the ammunition and to go to the meadow. So judging by that, I conclude that he was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That Gojko Simic was the leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct to you a time that you provided a statement to Jean-Rene Ruez. And I notice in your statement it says that, "I saw a group of seven or eight men who obviously did the shooting. They were standing not far away from the backhoe and were dressed in camouflage uniforms." Can you tell us, did you actually see them or did you just hear them? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard them, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then after that there's a statement that says, "Among them, I'm absolutely sure that I recognised a Serb who used to work with me. His name is Gojko Simic." Now, the term "recognised" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I recognised him by his voice and by the name I heard called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened after the discussions that the soldiers had among themselves where they talked about going over to another field? What's the next thing you recall happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they left, the loader came with the lights on. The excavator had the lights on too, but they were turned in the opposite direction. When this loader came, it stopped next to the backhoe and the two of them talked. I didn't hear what they said. Then the person who was probably closest to the loader and who was still alive, he jumped off and ran into the woods. They shot after him and the person on the loader turned the lights around towards the woods, probably to light him up, and at that moment, I moved. He cried out, "Here's another man who's escaping." I looked around a little bit but they weren't going towards me. So crawling, I reached the embankment next to the rail track. I looked around, no one was following me. When I jumped to my feet, I had to run up hill. It was like going up to the first floor, but it could have been the embankment along the rail track. I know that they fired some shots, but I didn't feel any bullets close to me, nor was I hit, luckily. I ran across the rails, I fell over the other side, then I got up again. There was a cornfield there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions if I could. Can you tell me when you were first able to actually see anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took the blindfold off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was that in relation to the events that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been two or three hours after this tragedy. When it was really dark and they had moved away from me, I took off the blindfold and I crawled from under the bodies that were on top of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to actually see these machines that you've talked about with their lights on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The machine that came with the lights on, it arrived just before I was -- I got up and ran away whereas the excavator was probably there before I had arrived, and its lights were turned in the opposite direction so that the back side of the machine was facing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But were you actually able to see those machines without your blindfold on when you crawled out from under the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The excavator you're talking about or backhoe, did that have tracks on it or wheels or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wheels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe it, as best you can, this thing you are calling an excavator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the loader? It was yellow; because building machinery in our country were, as a rule, yellow in colour the trademark was KU 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now you've described something that was called an excavator and you've described something that you called a loader. Those were the two machines that you've talked about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did the loader look like besides being yellow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front, it had the actual loader to collect the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's like a big bucket that can scoop up material and load it in the back of a truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The excavator, can you describe what the excavator looked like, how it was different from the loader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The excavator has a longer fork and it is used for digging big holes in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It has a big, long arm that can bend and has a bucket in the bottom of it and usually digs by pulling it backwards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It goes like this and then it turns backwards towards itself again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had described your narrow escape from this immediate spot. Can you go on and continue to tell us where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I ran into the corn half way, I went upright and then I fell down to the ground, afraid of rifle fire. So on all fours, I went through the corn and then I arrived in an area where I could hear water, but I couldn't see it. Serb soldiers that were left behind, they fired a few shots into the maize and I heard a few words exchanged. Further down, I only heard the shooting. When silence fell, I started thinking where I should go because I didn't know where I was as I was brought there blindfolded. I got up and started walking. When I came out of the corn, I was terribly afraid I might come across them somewhere. So I climbed on to the rail track and started walking along it slowly. I reached a railway station. There was an office that was open there. There was nothing inside. So I concluded I was going in the wrong direction. I could see a village down there. Then I went back again. I retraced my steps and I kept thinking where I should go. I came across a road where I saw that other location where men had been executed in the meadow. It seemed to me that one of them showed signs of life, but there was no hope. He was squealing like an animal, and he was slightly removed from the others. I still didn't know where I was. So I thought I should go into the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions, excuse me. Now, when you left that railway station, you started walking back in the original direction had you come from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was going the other way because I know if I went along the rail track to the right, I would be going to the same place and if I go left, I would be going in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you were generally heading in a similar direction as to where you came from but not precisely back to where you had been shot at; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. I was going back in the direction from which they had brought us. But if you cross to the other side, if you take the left tracks, you go towards Grbovci, and if you take the right-hand tracks you were going to the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you came back to the area where this man was still dying, was it still dark out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. It was still dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers or any equipment around this one spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to make out anything in the darkness about how many people were on this field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of bodies and clothes. There was moonlight so I could see them, but I didn't get closer than 20 metres away so I couldn't tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell where this field was in relation to the field where you had been shot at and shot down with the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't very far, maybe 100 or 200 metres only. It was on one side of the track.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This second site that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a stream nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this second site that you saw was on the other side of the railroad tracks from the area that you had been shot down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the other side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This summer, did you have a chance to go back to this area with Mr. Ruez and the investigative team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the place that -- Mr. Ruez first took you to the school, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The school that he took you to, did you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go in it, into the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the gym, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the place Mr. Ruez took you, the school in the gym, the same place that the Serb soldiers had taken you back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same gym and the same school. Everything was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after Mr. Ruez took you to the school, did he take you out to some fields nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise those fields that Mr. Ruez took you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did, because there's the field and the maize, and the maize was still there. Maybe this autumn somebody cut it, but the old maize is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What other distinctive features did you notice this summer when you went back with Mr. Ruez, that you recognised from your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my assessment was that there was this slope I had to climb to reach the rail tracks, and I recognised that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see railroad tracks at this site this summer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the site where you were shot down, was that closer to the asphalt road or farther away than the other site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further aside from the road, on the other side of the tracks. They were on the other location, on the mown meadow, which was closer to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after -- let me take you back now to July of 1995. It's still dark out. You've just come across this other field of bodies. Were you able to escape into the night and later escape to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't escape to the free territory on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many days did it take you wandering through the woods until you were able to escape to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have reached the area within two hours, if I had known, if I had known it, if I had known my way, but I kept wandering for at least ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then did you finally make it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you by yourself the whole time or did you have any -- run into any company, any friendly company, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was by myself all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Witness L, now you are going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Petrusic, who is representing the Defence in this case. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness L. Witness L, while you were living in Srebrenica, you were not engaged in the military in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you living together with your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we lived together; not before the war, but after the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your brother was in the military; he was there as a cook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness L, if you could please pause before you answer my question, because there are interpreters who have to interpret everything we say here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from your brother about a possible fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything from him. Nobody knew five or six days before it happened that it would fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of July the shelling started. Did people at that moment start to talk about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So on the 11th of July you reached Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said in evidence that the commanders had decided that you should go through the woods.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether they were military commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were both military commanders and personnel who was working at the Srebrenica municipality. They were also some kind of commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So would that include both political and military leaders of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they say anything about the population, the people who were supposed to go to Potocari and the people who were supposed to go to the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything about that, but we knew that Srebrenica had over 40.000 inhabitants, and therefore I think that there were about 15.000 able-bodied men, including young men, who didn't dare go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After you had spent the night between the 12th and the 13th of July somewhere in the woods around the area of Buljim you surrendered on the 13th of July, around 3.00 in the afternoon, to the VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your column, according to what you have said, had about 200 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my estimate, my column had about 400 people, but not everybody came with me; some people had arrived even before, and they kept coming afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the evening, after General Mladic had spoken to you, and before the buses and trucks had arrived, the buses that you later on boarded to go in the direction of Bratunac, how many people could have been on that meadow at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least 2.000 people. The meadow was crowded with people. People were sitting next to each other. There were between 30 and 40 rows -- the rows were between 30 and 40 meters long.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did everybody go in the direction of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not everybody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You were in the trailer of one of the trucks. Could you tell us how many people were put on the buses and trucks at that point in time, when you sat out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell you anything about that. I didn't know how many people there were. I don't remember the figures. The moment I entered the truck, I didn't know what was happening with other people. My brother had stayed behind, and I never saw him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness L, as you were coming down the hill, going towards the road where you eventually surrendered, did you notice any vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw several artillery vehicles, two or three of them, when we reached the road. There was an APC near the place where we were, and that's all, aside from the buses and trucks that kept passing by carrying women and children to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the meadow for a second. Could you observe any other groups of people from the spot where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could only see that one group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You saw some insignia, some patches with Republika Srpska Army letters written on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we saw one person wearing a kind of black scarf. He seemed to be in charge, and he was the one who told us that we would be exchanged. And he had a white patch on his sleeve, with letters VRS, Republika Srpska Army, on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In addition to the letters, Armija Republika Srpska, was there anything else on that patch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they had the four letters S, but it was difficult for me to observe that. And also their patches seemed to be damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness L, you testified that there were four young boys in the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those children were set free, because after I had reached the free territory I inquired about the release of the four young boys, and they told me that they had been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I can see in the transcript that the witness has mentioned four letters S. In the French interpretation I was told that the letters were written in Cyrillic alphabet, which I cannot see in the English transcript. Yes, but I still think it's very important. Perhaps, Mr. Petrusic, you could ask the witness if the letters were written in Cyrillic alphabet or in Latin alphabet. I think it is important, so if you could please do that, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will heed your advice and I will ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness L, you mentioned four letters S. Were they written in Cyrillic or Latin alphabet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs always used Cyrillic alphabet. Even their registration plates were in Cyrillic letters. And it was actually the first time that I saw registration plates in Cyrillic alphabet, which had not been the case before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a vehicle that you referred to as tamic. It was the vehicle that was near the gymnasium. You were put on that vehicle and taken to the execution site. You said that it had had civilian registration plates.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say anything about civilian registration plates. Whether they were police or military, I don't know. I'm not sure about the letter. I don't know whether it was the letter P. Because the Zvornik registration plates started with letters Z or V, so that was not a registration plate from Zvornik. So it must have been a police or a military vehicle. But it was a tamic vehicle with the green canvas on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So according to your observation, the plates started with Cyrillic letters ZV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was something like a letter P or a similar letter to that one. At any rate, it did not have ZV letters on it. This is what I had observed prior to that. And this time I could only see Cyrillic letters SC, the Serbian Sarajevo. But that was the vehicle which I had seen before that. But this one did not have a civilian licence plate. It could only have been a military or a police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My intention was not to confuse you. I just wanted to ascertain that the letter on it was P.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm telling you that I'm not sure. All I know is that the letters were not ZV.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you were brought to the execution site, the group of soldiers that was there waiting for you, was that the same group of soldiers who later executed people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, because they were not rotating. I could only hear shots, and I'm not sure whether those were the same soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they talk amongst each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at that time they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may, I should like to go back to a particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the witness whether at that time he could distinguish between police and military licence plates.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I wasn't familiar with the plates that were used by the Serbian police, but I think that they were not just either police or military. I still don't know what kind of licence plates the police had in the Federation or in Serbia, and in the Federation today we have a uniform type of licence plate, and so I don't know the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have concluded my cross-examination, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask two questions back at the gym that I failed to ask the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you forgot to ask those questions, then later on I will have to give Mr. Petrusic the opportunity to cross-examine again. Yes, please, do ask your questions, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While you were at the gym that was crowded with people, did you see any of the Muslims pass out in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were people passing out, mostly because they were thirsty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. Nobody helped us. But one of our people would usually go to get some water and we would ask that person to then give him some water to refresh him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the Serbs provide any sort of medical help at the gym at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none, whatsoever. No help at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have anything in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like to check whether I understand the witness correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When these people fainted, was it -- were they allowed to get some water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but because everybody -- the place was so crowded, and the water sometimes couldn't reach them and everybody asked for more water than there actually was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning Witness L. I'll just try to understand more clearly certain things you mentioned. You mentioned that you were captured with your brother. Did you hear anything about your brother since you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard anything. He went one way and I went the other and I don't know anything about what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Since the 11th of July, 1995, he has not --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the 13th of July, 1995, I haven't heard of him. Since that -- from the time when we were sitting together in the meadow. He was maybe 10 to 15 rows behind me sitting on that meadow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you try to make any search to find out? Did you get any news?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we searched for him through the Red Cross. He has a wife and children, but they were unable to locate him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you left Srebrenica to Susnjari, you said you had with you something like 200 armed men. Was there any exchange of fire between these men and between the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, no. I don't know what happened further on along the way. It was only later on that we learned that there had been an ambush, so they had remained behind and we left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: An ambush, who made the ambush for the other? Was it the Serbs who ambushed the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then, I'm just following your testimony, apparently some -- when Arkan's men came and they were -- you were asked to shout or to sing, "Long live the king." Who was that king?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably the Serbian king. We don't have a king at all. And the Serbs have a king. I mean, they don't have him now, but they used to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't know what they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't know which king they are referring to; last century, last --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Most probably -- now they don't have a king in Serbia, and there is no king in Bosnia either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you don't know. And when you were boarding the bus, you said you asked -- you answered the Defence counsel that the badges were damaged, you could not see their badges of the soldiers but you could hear their voice. You being a man living in that area, was it the Bosnian accent? Was it the Serb accent? What was the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they probably spoke with a Serbian accent which is even more pronounced now, but before they used to speak like us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The soldiers spoke like you or like the Serbs in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They spoke like us, but they have a slightly different accent. They pronounce -- they don't use the letter H every time they should, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who doesn't use the letter "H"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well Serbs, for example. We say "hljeb" and they say "ljeb", especially people from the countryside. But those living in cities, they speak like us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Those living in cities like Belgrade, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. There was no difference between Belgrade and places in Bosnian, but it also depended on the education. Educated people do pronounce this letter "H", uneducated people don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And these soldiers were educated people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know them. I know only this one who used to work with me as concrete reinforcer; he was a semi-skilled worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm speaking of soldiers. At a certain stage they are saying, "We are not soldiers, we are Karadzic's young Chetniks." Where did these young Chetniks come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were standing at the door of the gym where we were. They were sort of guarding us. They would shoot from time to time in the air. They were very young people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were most probably Bosniaks, Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you surrendered on the July 13th, you heard somebody saying, "These guys are ours." That was the translation. What was the meaning of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to my opinion, those elderly people most probably thought that if we were to be incarcerated, that then they could beat us because they didn't have any weapons in their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean you are their victims, "These guys are ours," means they want you to be their victims. Is that what you understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. Yes. Yes, this is what I understood them to mean that they beat us physically because they didn't have any rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And also at a certain stage you mentioned that Gojko Simic had said he would kiss all those who had been killed. What was the meaning -- what was the meaning of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that he would kiss the person who will speak. He wanted actually to discover whether anyone was alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when he kisses them, what will happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. You haven't understood me. He wanted to see whether anyone was alive and, of course, he would kill that person. He wouldn't kiss him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because there is something, you know, called the "kiss of death" if you want to save someone. So he wanted to kill them all. It was to kill them completely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they didn't want to let a single soul living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he kiss you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, it was interesting you mentioned that a woman, a Serb woman was in camouflage and gave you water. Were there women among the Serb soldiers killing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only woman. She was in the gymnasium from where we were taken, and I didn't see any woman over there and I didn't hear a female voice either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But she was not killing, she was giving water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was giving water. I don't know what her intentions were though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: My last question: You were mentioning that the registration on vehicles was in Cyrillic and it was not familiar in Bosnia. Did I understand rightly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before the war, the plates used to be in Latin alphabet, and everybody had the same kind of plates regardless of the nationality. But when the war broke out and until 1995, until I was captured at Grbovci, I didn't see that the Serbs had different plates, but at that moment I saw that they actually had different licence plates with Cyrillic letters on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness L.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness L, at the time that you were discussing the different kinds of uniforms and camouflage uniforms that the people around, I think it was the Grbovci school were wearing, I think that you were mentioning that some were wearing a grey camouflage that you thought were either Serbian Bosnian police or military. My question is: Did the people wearing those kind of uniforms do anything different? Were they performing different functions from the soldiers or were they doing the same thing as the soldiers in the regular army camouflage uniforms? Did they seem to be having a different function or were they intermixed with the army performing the same kind of guarding and transporting functions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were just there in the compound. They were mixed together, the Serb police and the army. But at the door were only soldiers, very young boys under 20 years of age, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But the ones who were in the yard with the greyish uniforms were basically doing the same thing as the other soldiers, right? They were not at the door, I understand they were in the yard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the yard when we arrived, but those in grey uniforms didn't come to the door because their police wear such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Could you tell what they were doing there? Were they just standing around? Were they doing anything special, the ones in the grey uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were just giving us orders to run towards the school, and we don't know what they did afterwards outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did some of the vehicles that you were discussing whether they had military or other kinds of police identification on it, were any of those kinds of military police vehicles used for transporting the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the vehicles were not like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You did speak of there being -- when you were being transported to the school, 30, approximately 30 large vehicles of all different types, you said. Could you tell whether all of those vehicles looked like they were local vehicles or did any of them have markings which would suggest they had come from farther away since there were so many large vehicles in that small place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the vehicles were civilian. None of them came from the outside. We would only see the vehicle that would be unloaded in front of us, then they would go back to pick up some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you couldn't tell whether some of these vehicles had markings of, you know, private companies on them or military markings or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have private or military markings. They were mostly vehicles from the former Yugoslavia, the socialist republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a company from Sarajevo, they had the same markings. The only difference being that the licence plates were in Cyrillic with a double "S" standing for Srpska Sarajevo, Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So some of them did come at least from towns and cities that were away from Grbovci and from where they were. They had to come a distance obviously if they came from Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they used those buses in Zvornik or Bratunac or Sarajevo, I don't know. I just know that those were the registration plates and that they were Centrotrans buses, belonging to the Centrotrans Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the Centrotrans Company, do you know whether it operates; all of Bosnia or just certain regions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of Bosnia and Herzegovina, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My next question is: In the Grbovci school when you went into the gym, could you tell whether or not that school looked like it had recently been used as a school, I mean, or was it an abandoned kind of school, a derelict school so that it didn't look as if it had been used as a school recently? Were things pretty well cleaned up so that it looked like it had been a regular school recently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until before the war, it was a regular school. But then afterwards when the war came, it was allowed to go into disuse so the gym wasn't up to something, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it didn't look as though that school had been used as a school in recent months or in the recent year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it probably hadn't been used for the past two years prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness L, I have two questions for you. The first is the following: While you were under the control of soldiers or the Serb army, how many days did you go without food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there around 22 hours. No one gave us anything to eat. I'm not counting the time when we went to be executed; I'm just counting the time that we were sitting there. Nobody offered us any bread or anything. Nobody asked for anything either, but nobody gave us anything either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question is the following. When you arrived at the school, that is, the gym, you saw a pile of clothing. I'd like to ask you: When you entered the school itself, when you got inside, was the school already full or was it still empty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was half full, more than half full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than half of the school was full?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for answering all our questions. You answered questions from the Prosecution, the Defence, the Judges. Is there anything that you would like to say and that hasn't been covered by the answers to the questions? If you wish to add anything, you may do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could just put a question to counsel, but one that is not linked to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm afraid not. You can leave the question in the air, but the attorney is not obliged to answer that question. You may put the question just like that, to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My question would be just for this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. lawyer, you are defending a man who left 50.000 children orphaned, without one or both parents. Don't you feel guilty for those orphans, and what right do you have to defend him? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to answer that, Witness L. The Defence attorneys are doing their job here, and they're doing their job properly. All the accused have the right to a Defence, and that is why we are here. We are here to hear the Prosecution and the Defence, and it is always important that the Prosecution does its job well, and the Defence also do their job well, and the Judges are there to judge. Thank you very much for coming here and for the spontaneous manner in which you answered our questions. I hope I will help you understand that all the attorneys are doing their job, which doesn't mean that they share any responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And regardless of the responsibility of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and regardless of the perpetrators of acts, and those acts are certainly horrible acts, and you are alive to tell the world that such acts must not be repeated. Don't move for the moment, Witness L. I think Mr. McCloskey has at least one exhibit to tender, Exhibit 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we would offer that as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Exhibit 100 will be tendered into evidence. Witness L, you have completed your testimony. Thank you very much for coming. And as I have told you, you must tell the world, you, who have lived through these experiences, that we should do everything to prevent a repetition of such acts. And please remember that all the accused are presumed to be innocent until proven guilty. That is the spirit of justice, and we are rendering justice here in the best way we can. So don't move yet, because you are a protected witness. We're going to have a 15-minute break now. And I think the next witness has more or less the same protective measures, so we will work in open session. So don't move, Witness, please. Good-bye, and we'll have a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Could you please stand up, because you have to read the solemn declaration first, which is written on the piece of paper that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now. Are you comfortable, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be treated well here. You are testifying before the International Tribunal and you will first answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. There is something that we have to take care of first. The representative of the Registry will show you a piece of paper with your name written on it, Witness. Could you please tell us by saying only yes or no if this is really your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now you will be answering questions. I'm sorry, Mr. Cayley. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, throughout your testimony I shall refer to you as Witness M in order to ensure that your identity is not disclosed. And if I could ask you to try to remember to speak as slowly as you can -- I know it's your manner to speak quite quickly -- because we have interpreters between us who are interpreting everything into English and French. You're a Bosnian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think until 1993 you lived in the area of Cerska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think in March of 1993, when Cerska fell, you moved to a village inside what became the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to now move forward in time, and I want you to think about the 11th of July, 1995. And I think at that time you and the other men from the Srebrenica enclave gathered at Susnjari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, where did the women and children go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The women and children went to Potocari, together with the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did the men not go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The men, the able-bodied men, didn't go to Potocari; they went to the woods, because they didn't dare to go into their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I may ask you questions the answers to which appear perfectly obvious, but nevertheless the Judges need to know. Why didn't you dare go to Potocari? Why did the men not dare go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I didn't dare go to Potocari, for example, because they had already surrounded us. They had surrounded Srebrenica and they were entering Potocari, and I didn't go there, didn't dare go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you refer to "they" -- you said that "they" had surrounded. Are you referring to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: They had attacked us, and on the 11th they entered the town of Srebrenica. And when that happened, I went to the woods, because I didn't dare go to Potocari. But I had sent my wife, my mother, and my children and a cousin of mine who was 14 years of age; he went to Potocari. They all went to Potocari. But he didn't survive. And we went to the woods. And my father was also sent to Potocari, but he preferred to go with us. He said, "Sons, I will go to you and then be what may."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it the Bosnian Serb army that had entered Srebrenica and surrounded the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: As they were entering the town of Srebrenica, I had already started towards the woods, together with the military. The command of the army ordered the able-bodied men to go through the woods; and those who were weak, they were supposed to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you in the army at the time yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you carry weapons with you on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No. We didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you remember approximately what time you left Jaglici on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: In the evening of the 11th of July, around 10.00 p.m., and this is where we lined up. This is where we assembled in Susnjari, and then we went in the direction of Jaglici, Pobudze, and Cerska, on onwards towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to move ahead in time to the 13th of July of 1995, when I think you found yourself on a hill called Dolina, which is between the hamlets or villages of Jelah and Krke. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 120. If it could be placed in front of the witness and then placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recall yesterday, you and I drew a sketch map of this area together and then this map that you see in front of you is generated on a computer today. Does this accurately reflect the sketches that you made for me yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is a correct drawing, correct representation of the location where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you place a copy on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you indicate on the ELMO, the location of Dolina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is Jelah here [indicates]. Krke and Dolina is here and this is where I was on a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 120 that the pyramid, the triangle, the black triangle is Dolina and that hill is in between two villages called Jelah and Krke.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, how far were you from the road that goes between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje? As the crow flies, how far were you from that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is Konjevic Polje [indicates]. Nova Kasaba is here and I was here near the asphalt road; 500 metres as the crow flies, maybe not even 500. So I could observe from the hill, the area of Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, I could see the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, from the hill at Dolina, can you tell the Judges what you recall seeing on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, it was a Thursday, I remember very well. It was about 2.00 in the afternoon and I noticed trucks and buses passing by moving from Konjevic Polje towards Nova Kasaba. I was there together with eight other people and people started to shout. They were saying, "They're probably taking our women and children. To the free territory." There were two or three buses there at that point and they turned right off the asphalt road and they went into the -- in the direction of Cerska across the bridge and I was watching them. There was a little path towards Skurici, but then they went directly to Cerska and they turned around the curve and this is where I lost them. There was an APC following them and two other trek vehicles. Maybe five or ten minutes after that, a yellow backhoe started out in the same direction and I could watch it travel as well and at that point, we could only hear fire of small firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could pause there for a moment. Now, you said in your evidence that you saw two or three buses which turned right off the asphalt road and they went in the direction of Cerska across the bridge. Can you indicate to the Judges, on the map on the ELMO next to you, the road that those three buses took?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The buses left Konjevic Polje and they turned towards Kamenica. There was a bridge here [indicates], you can see it here, across the Jadar river. And they moved up hill from there towards Cerska. There is a little road which turns left to Skurici they went towards Cerska and I could still see them. They turned right towards Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 120 that the three buses turned onto a road that goes towards the village of Cerska over a bridge that is indicated by a bridge symbol on that road, past -- turning to another small village called Skurici and on the way to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you also stated that you saw other vehicles following. Can you describe the APC that you saw to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I can describe the APC. I noticed also a trek vehicle that was green in colour. There was some soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms on that vehicle, but I couldn't tell which uniform it was. I didn't distinguish between various colours, but the soldiers were on the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also said, Witness, that you saw a yellow backhoe vehicle following these buses and the APC. Is that a vehicle which has a shovel on the front of it? Is that the kind of vehicle that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that kind of vehicle. It was yellow. It had wheels and it had a bucket or a shovel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you then said in your evidence that you heard infantry weapons firing. Now, prior to that, did you lose sight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, first of all, we heard small arms fire and then later on, we heard echo of other weapons that were being fired in the valley. And after the shooting stopped, this lasted for about half an hour, the three buses came back and took the same road in the direction of Konjevic Polje. And the APC followed them, but the excavator remained there longer, longer than half an hour. But it came back the same -- along the same road and it went also in the direction of Konjevic Polje following the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want you to think back to when you first saw the vehicles going towards Cerska. Was there a time when you lost sight of the vehicles because the road goes into woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, towards the woods, there was a wood there and I couldn't see them because they had turned around the curve and they went in the direction of Cerska. I could follow them for a while while they were passing through the valley, but I couldn't tell exactly what kind of bus it was, what company it belonged to. There were some letters but I couldn't make them out. I was on the hill, I was far away from the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In terms of the period of time that passed between you losing sight of the vehicles and the shooting starting, can you estimate now, looking back, how much time passed between those two events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The buses went away and after about 10 or 15 minutes, we saw the personnel carrier and then the excavator. And then they came back, one after the other. The personnel carrier followed the buses, but the excavator remained there a little longer. It lagged behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question. Do you recall that you stated that there came a time when the buses and the excavator and the APC disappeared from your sight into the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: They didn't go into the woods, they followed the buses along the same road and I could see them. First, the buses went, then the personnel carrier, then the yellow loader. They all followed the same road, and I could observe them until they turned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After the time that you couldn't see them anymore, how long after that time did the shooting start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The shooting started 10 minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 11/3. And if that map actually could be left there because we need that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a photograph that I showed you this morning. And what I'd like you to do is to show it to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the photograph be moved to your left, please. No, other direction and down a little. Actually, the other way slightly. And if you could just followed up there is a bit that's pressed down at the top of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you show to the Judges the hill at Dolina where you were watching these events from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Let me show you. This is Konjevic Polje, this is Nova Kasaba and this is where I was, at this hill, here, [indicates] this is where I was near the woods, the Krke woods. And from my vantage point, I could see the road leading to Nova Kasaba and the field beyond the road. This is the Krke wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just put your pointer on the location on the hill and leave it there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is the spot [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you show me the road to Cerska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is the road [indicates]. This is the bridge across the Jadar river and the road goes on towards Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm going to attempt to put this into the transcript. On a large panoramic photograph, Prosecutor's Exhibit 11/3, the witness has identified that he was about halfway up the most prominent hill in the middle of that photograph, and that he also indicated on the same exhibit, the road which runs in a vertical, near vertical fashion, from that hill and the main, I think, landmark is a bridge which he identified as a bridge across the river Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, what was your view like from the hill at Dolina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I had a very good view.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you grow up in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'm familiar enough with the area. If I didn't know the area, I probably wouldn't go there, but I had known the area from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think 16 days after Srebrenica fell, you managed to cross the asphalt road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The Serb army withdrew on the 14th day. The asphalt road was cleared and it was on the 16th day that we managed to pull through towards Macesi. That is the area between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba, not far from the turning towards Cerska, and this is where I crossed the asphalt road and I reached the woods near the area of Macesi. And this is where I found several other people. It was already dark. It was at nightfall, and it was drizzling and we spent the night there and after that, we went towards the Udrc mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness if you just wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 120 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, and if you could just show the Judges the village of Macesi and where you spent the night that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is Konjevic Polje and this is the road to Cerska and this is where I crossed the road between Konjevic Polje and Cerska halfway through and I went to cross the field and I went to the Macesi woods and this is where I spent the night. And after that I set out towards the Udrc mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I just have to record in our record what you pointed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness indicated that he crossed the tar macadam road and then turning off towards Cerska and then he proceeded towards a village which is marked as Macesi, spelled M-a-c-e-s-i on Prosecutor's Exhibit 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you then said that you set out towards the Udrc mountain and I wonder if you could just point out for the benefit of the Judges so that we don't all get lost in the forest the location of that mountain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is Udrc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And let the record show that the witness is indicating to a black triangle underneath which is the word "Udrc." The location is Udrc, just below the Drinjaca river.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you got to the Udrc Mountain, who did you find there, and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I found there quite a number of men, and I and my friends joined them. I came across a man with a nickname. He wrote down everything: what had happened along the way and what he saw. He put it all down in a notebook. And he listed all our names there on this mountain, our names and surnames, and said, "I'm going to cross into free territory, or at least my notebook will, and you stay here," and he took down everything. He wrote down the names. At that moment three men, two of whom were deaf and dumb, and we asked them how they had managed to escape from Susnjari and Jaglici. We approached them. And the man who was writing down everything, he approached them and asked them how had they managed. And then this man said, "You know where I'm coming from." And he said, "I'm coming from an execution site." I couldn't believe him. Surely it isn't true. And he said, "It is," and he showed me his trousers -- he lifted his trousers and he showed me his wounds. And then he pointed to his ears, saying that he could no longer hear from the explosions. He said he was coming from a hangar. Whether it was Kravica or another place, I'm not sure, but I managed to save my life and to escape. And he came to Udrc. And this man who went to free territory, who was going to free territory, he said, "Stay here and someone will come for you." We waited for him for 25 days. He didn't come. It started raining. We got off the mountain to a village. We lit a fire. There were just the ruins of a house and stables. We lit a fire to dry ourselves. There was some fruit: apples and plums, and pears, whatever we could find. It was August, I remember well, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if I could just interrupt you. Now, you've told the Judges about an account that was told by an old man, about how he and two disabled people managed to escape from Jaglici. Do you recall any other accounts that were given by people who had escaped from Jaglici, anything else that the man with the nickname wrote down in his diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I remember the eight men who also spoke about the mass grave. That night, on the 13th, they came along the road. They followed the same road as the APC. They followed that road, the macadam road, towards Kasaba. They said, "We took that road." And when we reached the crossroads we came across a pool of blood. When we saw that pool of blood, we didn't dare go on towards Cerska, so they turned towards Macesi. And the man who wrote this down asked them, "Where could this spot be?" They said, "I don't know." And I said, "If you can't remember the name, then say it was by the Uvalic house." And he wrote all this down. After that, maybe a month later, in September, I was looking for salt, me and my three friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if we could just -- I just have a few questions about what you just said. Now, you said that these men who told the man with the nickname about the pool of blood, that they had crossed the road on the 13th. Would that be the 13th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The 13th of July, 1995, when the shooting was heard, that night they managed to cross the road and went along the road to Cerska, and that is when they came across this pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the road to Cerska, if you could just indicate to the Judges again -- I know you've done it previously -- the road, just the road, on which they found this pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is the road to Cerska, here [indicates]. There's a turnoff for Macesi and these are the Uvalic houses, and it must have been here. There were some tree stumps there. This is the road to Cerska. And a month later I found this mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just wait there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Witness has indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 120 that the individuals informed the man with the nickname that the pool of blood was on the road which goes towards Cerska, just after the turning to the village of Macesi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I think there came a time when the Serbs actually noticed all of you men on the Udrc Mountain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when that happened, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: He noticed us on Udrc in August. I remember well. It was a Saturday when we came down from Udrc. Me and my friends who were with me came down to these villages of Babici and others. They were all burned down. There were some houses still standing. We lit a fire. Just then I lit a fire. I found a pot, a bucket, to get some water to wash myself. I started washing myself in a stable. At that moment the people from the houses started fleeing into the mountains. They were saying, "Here are the Serbs. The Chetniks are coming." I ran out through the door and I could hear firing at the village. And the troops were coming from the right and from the left to capture us. I just managed to put on shorts. I was barefoot, and I climbed up the mountain. The men who went left or right I think were captured, but I managed to escape to Udrc. I spent a day or two there, not long. Then they withdrew from there and I continued along the road to Kladanj. When I got to Huberi I found some more men there. This is towards Sandici. I came across more people and I asked: How were things? And they said, "We can't pass. There was shooting from all sides and we got frightened. We didn't dare go on." We spent the night there and went back along the same road we had taken. And we came back to the place at Suljici, Babici, where I had washed myself. And on the way I came across two dead people. One was my relative and the other I couldn't recognise. We were in Babici, and these friends asked me, "Are you going with me to Srebrenica?" I said, "I'm not going back to Srebrenica for the life of me. I want to go to free territory." Then these friends separated from me. They went towards Srebrenica to look for food. And then I went from this village of Turmadzici and Babici and I came across a small river between Hakalasi and Hasanovici. I came across eight comrades that I knew, and I joined them and stayed there all the time until I crossed into free territory 130 days later; I think 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you say that you tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Cayley. I think the witness should be asked to speak a little bit more slowly. At least the French interpreters are having difficulty in following him.
