utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, I know it's your manner to speak very quickly, but if you could try and slow down, because, as I said to you, we have interpreters between us. So if you'd just take a breath while you're talking, then that will make your evidence much clearer for everybody. Now, Witness, you said that you returned from Huberi back to the Cerska area, and that you met some friends and you came across, I think, eight comrades, and you joined them and stayed near a small river. Can you indicate on the map where it was that you were staying at this time with your eight comrades? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Approximately. This is Cerska [indicates]. There's a road going to Hasanici and there's another road to the left, and I followed the river. And halfway between Hasanovici and Hakalasi I was there, between Hakalasi and Hasanovici, in the river. It's about 15 minutes from Cerska, from the school in Cerska, to this part where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not going to try to explain that into the transcript, but I think it would be accurate to say on Prosecutor's Exhibit 120, that the witness indicated that he stayed near a stream about 15 minutes from Cerska, which is marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, there came a time, I think, when you ran out of salt, and you and your comrades decided to try and go and search for food and for salt. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I do. It was in September, but I don't know the exact date. When we ran out of salt, we wondered what we should do. We had a little salt. We ate whatever we could: mushrooms, plants. So then we decided to go down to Pobudze, where we saw a lot of dead and a lot of backpacks. We thought we'd find some salt there. So the four of us set off from the mill and we reached the school at Cerska. From the school -- it was an eight-year elementary school. The four of us agreed at the school the two would look to the right, two to the left, to see where that grave could possibly be. And so from Cerska we went to Konjevic Polje, Kasaba, along the road. We followed the road and we were looking to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you indicate to the Judges the road you're talking about that you took from Cerska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is Cerska [indicates]. This is where the school is. And we went along this road. We went along this road towards Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating the road that goes from Cerska to the junction of the road between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could continue with your account of what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: When we left Cerska, the school, when we reached a crossroads called Talusa Luka, we found a pile in the grass, and the two of them said, "This is where the grave must be." We saw it wasn't a grave; it was somebody who had started building before the war. Then we went on and we got to this place, Masuska [phoen]. And then the two of them said, "Here is the grave." And we found it, right here [indicates]. When you go from Cerska, the tomb was on the left -- no, on the right. On the right-hand side was where the excavator had dug the earth. We saw the tomb with freshly dug earth over it. We were sorry. We cried. It could have been my son, my brother. They must be ours. Then he counted 25 steps long. The crater was about 25 steps long and 10 steps wide. I noticed the traces of a caterpillar, of the loader. From that grave, about 5.200 metres, is a road, a crossroads, going towards Macesi, and these houses had been mined, Uvalic's houses. I couldn't see any traces of blood, because there had been rain in the meantime. After that we went along this same road and we reached the bridge across the Jadar. And we didn't dare go towards Konjevic Polje or Nova Kasaba, so we went between Jelah and Krke, and I reached this hill called Dolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if I could just take you back. Could you point to the spot -- and I know this map is only approximate -- where the mass grave is located, where you found the grave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Here it is [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to a rectangle just below and to the right of Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you also said that you could see where an excavator had dug earth. Can you point on this map to where you saw the excavator digging earth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Right across the way, across the road from that grave, here [indicates]. We noticed the traces of the wheels. We saw the traces there, here, on the right-hand side of the road if you're going to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to a Chevron sign immediately above the black rectangle indicating the site of the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you now -- you said that there were two houses down from there that belonged to the Uvalics. Can you just point to those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Those were the Uvalics' houses, the two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to two house-shaped objects marked "Uvalic," immediately to the right of the spot marking the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, when you discovered this grave, did you smell anything there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I could tell by the smell, the stench. One could feel the stench.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now show Prosecutor's Exhibit 16/5, which is a video. And this, Your Honours, is the video that you've seen already of the Cerska Valley region. It's a heavily wooded area, it's very rugged, but I think it will give you a better idea of the area we're talking about. I've taken some video stills which the witness can identify. But it's about 1 minute 30 seconds, 1 minute 45, so it will remind you of the area that we're talking about. If the video could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where I was. That is where I saw the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has just indicated on the video which shows the road to Cerska, that that is where he saw the buses which he referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are the houses [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are those the houses that belonged to the Uvalic brothers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the two houses of the Uvalic brothers. And here's the tomb. This is where the tomb is [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 121, and this is a series of stills, Your Honour, that were taken from the video that we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you pointed out the houses of the Uvalic brothers, and they're just ruins. Why are those houses in ruins, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Those houses were all right while we were in Cerska. When Cerska fell, they went to mine and destroy one house after another, all our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs, you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs, yes, I'm talking about them. They destroyed, torched and mined our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point out on these photographs, first of all, the location of the houses of the Uvalic brothers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Those are the houses of the two Uvalic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating on the panoramic view in the frame that is to the furthest right in the series and you can see in the middle of that two grey-white areas which I think can be clearly seen on the clip below the remaining foundations of a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you show the house, the road to Macesi, the intersection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is the road to Cerska, and this is the road that goes to Macesi. You can see it here that's where it is. That's the road to Macesi from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My colleague has just informed me that I've misdescribed the photograph. In fact, the Uvalic brothers houses were on the extreme left in the frame, on the extreme left of the panoramic view, and you can see the two sort of grey-white areas which indicate the foundation of those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, can you point out the road again to Macesi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The road to Macesi, here it is, this is the crossroad and it turns off here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the witness has indicated in the panorama and it can be clearly seen that it goes out to the right and disappears out of the bottom right-hand corner of the panorama.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And finally, Witness, can you indicate the location to the Judges of the tomb or the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Here it was, here. This is where it was here [indicates]. There was a meadow here, the grave, the river, and this is where the earth was dug up. So the grave was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the witness is indicating on the frame on the right of the panorama and it is an area which is on the left-hand side of the road going towards Cerska as the road disappears out of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could look at the photograph below which is a clearer view of that final frame.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it can be seen here. This is the mass grave on the left when going to Cerska and this is where the excavator dug the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating in the single frame photograph on the lower right side of the exhibit a white-grey area in the centre of the photograph just above where the road curves down and goes off to the left is the grave, and that below that where there's a hedgeline is an area, I think he said, where the earth was dug, where the excavator dug the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Finally, if we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 16/3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is it [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the booth perhaps pan out somewhat. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you first of all indicate to the judges the site of the grave that you discovered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The site of the grave, this is where the grave was on this side [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating on Prosecutor's Exhibit 16/3 to the right of the yellow distance markers which run down the centre of the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is the road here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate to the Judges where you saw where the excavator had been at work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The excavator had been working on the right-hand side, the left -- no, the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate with your pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Across the way from the grave here [indicates] here, here somewhere. There was the slope up there [indicates]. This is the road [indicates], and this is the road to Macesi, this is -- to the right is the grave, and this is where they dug the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is showing that the excavator had been working on the side of the road which is essentially where the vehicles are parked, so directly opposite the mass grave and it is, in fact, on the left-hand side of the photograph as you look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. Can you tell the Judges who were the male members of your family that you lost during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: After 130 days, I reached free territory. It was the 18th of November when I reached Kladanj. I learned that I lost my father, my brother, cousins, my neighbours; and my father who I loved most. I have my mother, my wife, and children, no brother, no father, no 14-year-old nephew. They have disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And they -- all of these members of your family disappeared at the time of the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. I don't have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Visnjic, how much time do you think you will need for the cross-examination of the witness, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, maybe 20 minutes, and I was about to suggest a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We will have a 15-minute break now -- no, perhaps we should have half an hour break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness M, have you had some rest during the break?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you're going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Visnjic who is representing the Defence in this case. Let me just remind you, once again, that we speak two different languages and we risk having problems here. And the two of you, Mr. Visnjic and yourself, you speak the same language which can make things even more difficult. So I should kindly ask you to try and make breaks, make pauses between questions and answers so that the rest of us can hear you and understand you. Thank you very much. Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness M.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness M, let me go back to the beginning of your story. You said you had lived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, and I was in Srebrenica until the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the town itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I lived in the outskirts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you said at one point that on the 11th of July, when Srebrenica fell into Serb hands, that the population split in two groups; that one group went to Potocari and the other to Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Women and children, civilian population, went to Potocari, and the able-bodied men went to Susnjari in order to save their lives; some managed to do that, some didn't. I was lucky enough to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This division of the population was carried out according to whose orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, our soldiers, our military men were shouting, giving orders. They were telling us -- they told us that the women and children should go to Potocari, and those who felt healthy and well enough, that they should go to the woods. This is what our commanders told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did you personally learn about that? Was there a messenger who conveyed the order or were there just rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: We gathered in the village of Kazani near the cemetery in Srebrenica, and this is where they were told what had happened. They said that women and children and the elderly should go to Potocari, and those who were able-bodied, that they should go to the woods and try to save their lives in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said somebody had told you; was that somebody specific or were there just rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is what we heard. They were shouting and they were telling that the weak ones should go to Potocari and that the others should go to the woods, to Susnjari. And those were the orders, and some people survived, some didn't. I managed to survive. And so let me tell you once again, it was very difficult for us. I have not come here to argue with you. I have come here to tell the truth about what we have been through. And I have come to tell you about the 130 days that I spent in the woods and how I managed to survive. I've come here to tell the truth about what has happened to me. And I feel very sorry for the people. And this gentleman sitting here, if he had known for this Tribunal, he wouldn't have come here, would have lived -- stayed there and lived with us as he did before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness M, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but could you please try and answer Mr. Visnjic's questions in a direct manner. If a question is a direct one, please try to give us a direct answer. We are here to do justice and there are two parties here in this case. There is the Prosecution and the Defence. Everybody has the right to defence. Imagine if something should happen to you, you would also need somebody to represent you. We do understand the suffering you've been through, but please try to answer the questions of Mr. Visnjic directly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness M, in one of your previous statements, you said that the column had left Susnjari around 10.00 p.m.; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were walking from the 12th of July until 13th, that you reached the village of Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that is true this is where we spent the day resting, it was the place of Kamenica. And this is actually where the tragedy happened later on, the terrible thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please, if we can let the interpreters translate. This is why I stopped. You also said that you left Kamenica around 6.00 p.m. and that around 1900 you ran into an ambush; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. We were surrounded and they opened fire and the shooting lasted for about half an hour, and a disaster happened and people were in great fear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also said that on the 13th of July you arrived in the village of Burnice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in the morning hours of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Also on the 13th, that is, on the same day, you left the village of Burnice and went to village of Rahonjici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. We went across the field and we reached the village of Rahonjici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that on the same day you left the village of Rahonjici and went to the village of Mranice, which is near the village of Rahonjici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I did, and this is where I reached the junction where I found three or four dead bodies. The junction was the one for the village of Mranice and the village of Krke. And I heard somebody -- I heard noises, I heard people calling me, but I didn't dare move.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What day was it, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It was on the 13th, on Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you -- this all happened on Thursday morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also stated that a part of the people from your group surrendered on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. There were maybe 50 of us in the group, and there were some people whom I knew, whom I recognised. People were inquiring about their family members. And while I was there in that group, a personnel carrier came from Konjevic Polje, from the direction of Konjevic Polje. I couldn't recognise the soldiers who were on the personnel carrier, but I noticed that they were wearing camouflage uniforms. And they went in the direction of Nova Kasaba, but they only got as far as Dzugum, as far as a cafe which was situated there. And people started shouting, telling us to surrender. They were telling us that the Red Cross was there, that UNPROFOR people were there, and they told us to come down to the asphalt road and to surrender. I was there together with other people, but whoever had any wits about him didn't even think of surrendering. And some 130 of us remained in that river, in that little brook. And this is -- and then afterwards I went in the direction of Jelah and the Krke woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What time of the day was it when several members of your group surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It was on the same day, on the 13th of July, around 10.00 or maybe half past 9.00 in the morning. And I was watching them while I was at the village of Krke, as they were climbing down the hill and going towards the asphalt road. I noticed several groups of Serb soldiers and I could see people coming out on the asphalt road. I could hear Serb soldiers asking them if they had any weapons, and they said they didn't, and at that point they would raise their hands. But then one would hear a voice of someone who was giving commands, and then they told people to halt, to stop, and to raise their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How far were you from the asphalt road at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: There was a brook there and there was a little forest, the Krke wood, and maybe I was some 500 meters away from them. I'm not quite sure. This is an approximate distance. But I could see everything. I could see the asphalt road, I could see people coming down to the asphalt road, I could see them surrender, being captured. And the Serb soldiers also came down to the asphalt road and they were pointing their rifles at them, trying to prevent them from escaping, and I was observing all that. I wanted to see whether they would be taken to Kasaba or to Konjevic Polje. But I didn't follow them as far as Nova Kasaba. I lost them at one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I should like to ask you to ask very specific and short questions so that we don't lose too much time, waste too much time. The question was what distance it was. If you can try to control the witness, please, Mr. Visnjic. You can interrupt the witness. That's okay with me. If you don't do that, I will have to intervene every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't want to interrupt the witness, but otherwise I would have intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify something, Witness M. You were observing the asphalt road at the moment some people surrendered. You were at the same spot as when you saw the buses and the excavator.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No. I was closer to the location. I was in Mranice and I was between the Krke wood and the brook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So this is another location; this is a different location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. I was watching people coming down to the asphalt road and surrender from that wood, and I saw them leave in the direction of Konjevic Polje. And afterwards I left the Krke wood and I went in the direction of Jelah, and this is where I stopped, on a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us pause a little for the interpretation, and then I will ask my question. So this is where you were on the 13th of July, in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning. It was in the morning when I was at the Krke woods. And after that I left the Krke wood and I went to the area called Dolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What time was it when you reached this other location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It could have been 1.00, half past 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How far from you were the Serb soldiers, from the second location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, maybe 500 meters away from me. They were on the asphalt road and I was in the forest, and I was watching from my vantage point. I didn't want to move, because I was afraid. I wanted to stay near the brook. And I was actually running from wood to wood. I was hiding all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in the morning you were on a location which was some 500 meters away from the asphalt road, and you were afraid that you would be found by Serb soldiers, so you moved to another location, which was also 500 meters away from the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, and it was between Krke and Jelah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My next question concerns the second location. You could see Serb soldiers from that location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: From the second location where I was between Krke and Jelah, in the area of Dolina? No, I could not see soldiers from there, going towards Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you see Serb soldiers on the asphalt road from that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, because the road was completely blocked. People were coming down from the area of Mranice and Krke and going towards Konjevic Polje. That whole area was completely sealed off. Nobody could get through. And they had posted their guards every ten -- there were bunkers everywhere, every ten to fifteen --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me: You saw three buses on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, on the 11th, in the afternoon, around 1400 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were there Serb soldiers in those buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I couldn't notice whether Serb soldiers were in the buses or not, whether there were civilians or ordinary people. I don't know. I just saw three buses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you couldn't see whether there was anyone in the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Because I was far away, I couldn't see. It was a large distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that those buses were full of people, or is it your assumption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It is my assumption, because later on I heard the shooting. I'm not sure, but I think that those were the people who had surrendered. I assumed that those were those people who went to Konjevic Polje, in the direction of Cerska. That is what me and my comrades thought, that they must be those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness M, you made a statement previously to the Tribunal and the Ministry of the Interior after you crossed into free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. I told the truth everywhere. I made a statement, telling the truth, and I have come here to tell the truth, to tell everything I saw and experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I know that some time has passed by since then and that perhaps your memories are not too precise, but I would like to show you the statement you gave to the Ministry of the Interior on the 22nd of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D15.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 1 I have highlighted in yellow, to make it easier for you to find the place. There's a sentence which says: "On the 12th day, after I left Srebrenica, so that is on the 22nd of July, 1995, in the afternoon, from the direction of Konjevic Polje three white buses arrived, followed by an armoured personnel carrier on wheels, with an anti-aircraft gun on the turret and a yellow excavator loader." My question is as follows: During your stay in the area of Pobudze did you see three buses driving in the direction of Cerska on a number of occasions or only once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Only once, on the 13th of July, around 2.00 in the afternoon. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher for his assistance, please, with the next exhibit. It is a statement given on the 17th of January, 1996, to the investigator of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, excuse me for interrupting you. It's simply to tell you that the method that you used for the other exhibit is a very good one, so you can use it in the future as well. I'm just telling you that we appreciate that very much, so please do that in the future as well. So you can continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm afraid on this exhibit I failed to mark the sentence, and I accept your criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 4, fourth paragraph, it starts: "At 1400 hours --" Have you found the place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "At 1400 hours we saw three white buses full of people coming from the direction of Konjevic Polje, going in the direction of Nova Kasaba. I could not see if the passengers were only men, but I assume that they were transporting prisoners who had surrendered."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. That is correct. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the previous paragraph it says, "The 14th of July, buses and trucks packed with people were passing along the road." So can you explain the difference between these two events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. The people were going from Konjevic Polje to Kasaba in trucks and buses; in the morning too they were passing by, and I followed all this and I saw all this. When in the afternoon they went towards Cerska, I thought that they were also civilians that they were taking. But when I saw them turn towards Cerska, I said, "Something is wrong." No, but the other one said, "They're taking them to free territory," and I said no, and I proved to be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you didn't see whether they were full of people so you just assumed that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I assumed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness M, you stayed in the area, if I understood you correctly, until around the 25th of July for some 11 or 12 days in all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: After that, I couldn't pass. The Serbian army had withdrawn from the bunkers and freed the road, and I was able to pass. The first night I passed, they didn't fire. But we were all afraid, of course, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but let's answer the question, please. I assume that you were watching the road on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I was watching the road. Then I went back to the villages and hid in the woods. Another day the infantry started after us from Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Finally, you crossed to the other side and reached Udrc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. After that, I did. On the 16th or 17th day, I reached the Udrc mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During your stay on Udrc mountain, did you have any indications or did you hear that the Serb army was searching the area and following you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Of course they were following us and monitoring us. I noticed them all, yes, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How long did this last while you were on Mount Udrc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: When I crossed the asphalt road, that was the 18th day. I spent 25 days there on Udrc. This was in August when the army arrived and the APC. That was a Saturday at the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: For how long were they searching the area; for one month, two months, or did you have the feeling that they were there all the time? I'm not asking you about that specific event. I'm asking you, roughly, can you tell us an indication of the time they spent searching the area? Was it throughout the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: For a short time, no, only for about a few days, a short time. A short time, only two days. They were chasing people and those they managed to catch alive, and when they withdrew, then we came down and went through the woods. And later on I joined this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Later you didn't come across Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, never again. And I was able to move around freely in Cerska, my place. We were safe there. It was better in Cerska and on Udrc mountain than in Pobudze because I was encircled on all sides there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you did go back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did to Pobudze. I was looking for salt, we needed salt. There were dead people, our people, in the streams in the fields. And we searched their knapsacks to find some salt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This was at least a month later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, this was about mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the incident when you discovered the mass grave. As far as I understood from your testimony, you moved around quite freely in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. After the last search in August, we moved around freely in the woods and along the road. There were no searches, there was nothing, so we were free to move around in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you found that grave, did you just find a pile of earth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, fresh earth on the left-hand side of the road. And on the right-hand side, I saw where the excavator had dug up the earth and traces of the wheels and I felt the stench of corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see any corpses, you just felt the stench and the traces on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, I just had this smell, and we noticed those traces of the excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was there any grass covering that earth already or any weeds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, no. There was no grass, it was fresh. There was no grass on that earth, it was freshly moved earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cayley, do you have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no questions for the witness in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Judge Riad

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, do I have a number of questions. Good morning, Witness M. I would just like to start to ask you just a very few questions from where the Defence counsel stopped concerning the grave you found. You found the grave in September when you had left Cerska and it was freshly dug earth, but you felt the stench and you assumed there were dead people inside.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could these be the people who were killed in July, would they smell if they are still entered in September, or you assume that they would be freshly killed people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I assume they were the people who surrendered who went to Konjevic Polje, and I think they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But there were no signs of dead bodies on the ground, it was all under the ground.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I didn't notice any bones or anything like that, only the smell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the houses were mined, the Uvalic brothers', and other houses were torched and so on, you saw them around. Did you understand or know anything about the people inside? Were they mined with the people inside, some of them, or were they empty houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Those houses of the Uvalic brothers, they were mined after Cerska fell and the people were evicted. It was after Cerska fell that the houses were mined. When I had left Cerska, they were still standing; not just those two houses but the entire village of Cerska. It was later that the houses were mined and the people chased out and the burning was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand more about the buses you saw when you were going towards Cerska. I think both your testimony today as well as your statement indicates that you saw buses. You said there were three white buses with an excavator and APC, and you just counted almost the minutes you said they disappeared into the woods, and then the shooting started a few minutes later. And that they were full. You saw that they were full, but you did not see what kind of people were inside. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I didn't see whether the buses were full or empty, but I assume that there were people inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But for sure they were empty when they came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I'm sure they were empty when they came back. When the buses came back from up there, and the APC, and the excavator, the loader, I assumed that they had been full when I heard the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So when you were on this spot, what was exactly the scenario that you saw in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: When I followed those three buses along the road from Konjevic Polje, crossing the bridge and going up there, I assumed that there were people inside and that they were taking them to be executed, and that is what happened and we heard the shooting. And when the shooting stopped, the buses came back along the same route, and the excavator/loader stayed behind a little longer for about half an hour after the buses and the APC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. As far as the shooting was concerned, was it the shooting that was heard in a battle or was it shooting you would hear in some kind of systematic way which indicates execution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I heard very strong, heavy fire. It was very loud. It was -- there was a lot of noise, very heavy shell fire could be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean it was guns or cannons? What do you call "heavy fire"? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I think there were light arms and also machine-guns, bursts of fire from a machine-gun. One could hear it echoing along the valley. It was very loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But how long did it last approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: 15 minutes, half an hour, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And after the buses went back, there was no fire again, no bursts of fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, because probably the APC came after the buses, only the excavators stayed there a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned a man whom you met who was noting all that happened and he was coming from an execution site, he was a survivor of an execution. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That man at Udrc, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, did he tell any details about the execution he lived out of, the number of executed, who did the execution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: He told us then, and this man took everything down in a notebook, he said that he had escaped from an execution site. We didn't believe him. He showed us the wounds. It was either Lolici or Kravica in a hangar. That's what he said. He recognised a relative of his from Cerska and he gave his name, but he didn't know the others. That is what he told us. And he managed to escape the execution. And I didn't see him again. I don't know what his destiny was, whether he's alive or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the number of executed, he did not give you an indication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention numbers because he couldn't hear too well. Anyway, he was going deaf. He was showing with his fingers that he had gone deaf. That man was there with us until Udrc fell. I didn't see him again. Whether he crossed into free territory, whether he survived or not, I don't know. But he came to Udrc and he told me that he had come from this execution site. I can't remember exactly whether he said Lolici or Kravica, he didn't know exactly anyway, but he did say he had come from an execution site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, and you can answer it if you know anything. You mentioned on the 11th of July when the Serbs entered Srebrenica, the men preferred to go to the woods so not to be massacred, but the women and children went to Potocari. What happened to the women and children? Were they safe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The women and children went to Potocari and we, who were able-bodied went into the woods. I told my wife and mother, "Go to Potocari and look after the child, and I'm going into the woods. If I survive, fine. If not, who knows." I didn't know whether I would manage to cross into free territory. My father was there. He was born in 1932. And I and my brothers were telling him to go to Potocari, to go with the women, but the old man said, "I won't, I daren't, they may kill me. If you survive I will too. If you get killed, I get killed too. I'm not sure about going to Potocari." My nephew who was 14 or 15, he just said, "I'm going to Potocari with the women." But he didn't reach free territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And why didn't he reach it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Because I heard that there was a disaster there. They separated the young boys and they took them away and executed them as -- at their free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He was 14 years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, my nephew was 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to evoke these memories, but we have to know the truth. Thank you very much, Witness M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank Your Honours and everybody working on this. I have come just to tell the truth. And whoever is on the list of war crimes regardless of what ethnic group they belong to, they need to be arrested and tried and brought to court, to justice. If they had been good and if all those Serb soldiers had known about The Hague, they wouldn't have done what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness M, you still haven't finished your testimony. Judge Wald has questions for you so will you please answer them. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness M, you told us this morning that on July 13th, you said July 13th was the day that you saw the buses, the three buses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You said that when you first saw them, "some of the people", and I assume you mean some of the other men that you were with began shouting that these must be our women and children, that they're taking to Tuzla. Had you seen any buses that same day, that is July 13th, of women and children going on the road to Tuzla so that these people around you would assume this was another set of those buses. Had you already seen some buses on the road with women and children going in the direction of Tuzla on Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: On the 13th, I was watching everything and I saw everything; the buses and trucks going from Konjevic Polje towards Kasaba. We assumed that the people were going to Potocari, were being transported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But had you seen, previously, some other buses which you were sure, from your sight, did contain women and children either that day or -- I guess, that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: We assumed when those buses and trucks were going to Kasaba, we assumed that the people were being carried but the other three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that but referring to the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor, you had said you had a different date then. But leaving that aside, you said, "Buses and trucks packed with people were passing along the road. We could see that women and children were on board." So I was asking you although you didn't say that in your testimony today whether the reason the men around you assumed that these were women and children because they had actually seen prior buses of women and children such as you mentioned in your statement to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Those buses and trucks that were going towards Kasaba and the people who were with me, they were all saying that they were transporting women to free territory. But at 12.00 when they turned towards Cerska, I said, "They're driving them to execution." But I -- they said, "No, to free territory," but I said, "to execution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I understand that very well. I was trying to reconcile what you said previously in your statement that you had earlier seen buses and trucks, actually seen them with women and children on board and that's why people might well have assumed, to begin with, that these buses had women and children. But you don't remember that right now, right, whether you had earlier seen, actually seen buses with women and children. I know these were not the same.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Those three buses that went to Cerska, I said that they were men being taken to execution whereas the others were taking the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. When those three buses returned, when you saw them come back, returned, and you were sure that they were empty, where did they go? I mean when they passed by coming back empty, where did they go? What direction did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: They went in the direction of Konjevic Polje. They came from that spot in Cerska towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you about the statement that Defence counsel mentioned that you gave to the Ministry of the Interior. I notice that that was given on November 22nd. I believe that would be just four days after you came into the free territory since you said in your testimony you had been wandering and you had been in flight and didn't get over to the free territory until November 18th. So this statement in which you said that this all happened on July 22nd, not July 13th, was given only four days after you got back into the free territory after wandering around for months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I arrived on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That is true. And when I gave that statement, I was in Tuzla, on free territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, four days later. I was only bringing it up to see if you thought that might be the explanation for why, since you had just been into free territory for four days after wandering around for months, your sense of the time might not have been as accurate as your later memory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I remember giving that statement. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness, I think that was your final statement in a sense. I should like to tell you that we agree with you that regardless of ethnic origin, all people responsible of crimes should be judged, we agree with you. Because the acts committed do not change their horrible nature depending on the ethnicity of the perpetrators. They are always horrendous. Therefore, Witness M, thank you very much for coming and we wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I wish to thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't move now because we are going to have a 15-minute break, but before that, I should like to check whether we are having a witness with the same protective measures which means an open hearing, and there are some exhibits to regulate. Exhibit 120 and 121 of the Prosecution and Exhibit D-15 and D-16 of the Defence. Mr. Cayley, perhaps you could cover all the exhibits together, both of the Prosecution and the Defence. I think regarding the Defence exhibits, we have to bear in mind the need to protect the witness. So we would perhaps tender them under seal and have a redacted version open to the public. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree entirely with you in respect to the Defence exhibits. That's what I would have suggested what you've stated and I would simply apply for admission into evidence Exhibits 120 and 121, the exhibits of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Visnjic, in relation to all these exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objections regarding the exhibits of the Prosecution. We would just like to observe, to look through the statements. But I see that the name of the witness is indicated in handwriting on the top of the page, so it would be a good idea to scratch those names too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So exhibits are admitted bearing in mind the confidentiality of the exhibits. That is D-15 and D-16. We will have a version under seal and another after redaction open to the public. You will bear that in mind, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps you could bring the next witness into the courtroom during the break. So we're going to have a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness N. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please stand up. You will first read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now. The representative of the Registry will now show you a piece of paper with something written on it. It is your name. You will have a look at it and tell us, by saying simply "yes" or "no," if it is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is your name that is written on this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you're comfortable here, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you've been well treated by the staff here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall try to do the same, Witness N. We will be referring to you as Witness N during your testimony in order to protect you. You will first answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Harmon. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good a afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you lived in the municipality of Srebrenica all your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next two or three questions I'm going to ask the witness could in some way identify him, so if I could go into private session for two or three questions only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Mr. Harmon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, after the Srebrenica enclave -- after Srebrenica became --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- a UN safe area, did you remain in the Bosnian Muslim army or were you released from the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I was released. I didn't remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the time of the takeover of the enclave by the Bosnian Serb army, were you living --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, let me finish asking my question before you answer, and we will progress very nicely. At the time the enclave was taken over by the Bosnian Serb army, with whom were you living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: With my wife, my son, my daughter-in-law, a child, and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you live approximately 15 kilometers from the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness N, I'd like to focus your attention on the 11th of July and ask you to remember back to the 11th of July, and could you tell the Judges what you were doing at the time you learned of the attack on the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: On the 11th of July I was collecting hay, together with members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell the Judges, if you would, Witness N, how you learned about the attack and what you did in response to that information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: When I got home, I saw that my neighbours had gathered at one point, that they had taken their belongings, whatever they could carry, and I asked, "What is going on?" And they told me that somebody from the civil defence had come and told them to leave the village. Women, children and the elderly were supposed to go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari, and the able-bodied men were supposed to go wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, did you then go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And who accompanied you to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: My wife went with me, my daughter, my daughter-in-law, and my grandchild.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to get from your village to Potocari on foot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: It took us around three hours, over the hills to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Potocari in the night-time or in the daytime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: In the night-time I arrived in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember where you and your family took refuge in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We took shelter at the Sacmara factory, the bauxite factory, within the compound of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Witness N. Now I'd like to turn your attention to the next day, the 12th of July. And at some point of time on that day did you and did members of your family attempt to board a bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you were attempting to board a bus, what happened to you, Witness N?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Serb soldiers were standing next to our column, and they grabbed me by the shoulder and they told me, "Come here, old man. Get out of there."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what happened to your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: My family went in the direction of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they, in fact, board a bus and did they, in fact, arrive safely in the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: To the left side of the road, and I remained standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you taken to a particular building after you had been separated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: After they had gathered a group of people, 15 to 20 people, Serb soldiers told us that we could no longer stand there, and they told us to go up the hill to a partly finished house. And this is where we went. We entered the ground floor of that unfinished house and sat down, and they stood guard around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe how the soldiers who separated you and how the soldiers who guarded you at this location were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: They were dressed in green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, while you were in the building, were there other Muslim men also detained along with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many were located in the building, in the part of the building where you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: About 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At some point during the period of your detention in that building, did you see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell the Judges about that particular encounter with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: One of the Serb soldiers, after quite a few of us had gathered there and after we had asked him why we had been separated, told us, "I don't know. General Mladic is coming now, so you can ask him." And then an officer appeared. He wasn't wearing any hat, any cap. He had balding, receding hair. He emerged from the road and he was accompanied by three or four other Serb soldiers and he came to the door of the house where we were. And he said, "Hello, neighbours," and he asked us if we knew him. Some of us said yes, some of us said no. And then Ratko Mladic said, "Well, those who don't know me now have an opportunity to see me." And then I asked him a question: "General, why are you separating us from our families?" And he said, "I have 180 Serbs captured in Tuzla. Your people do not want to release them, so I have to have 180 of you so that I could exchange you for them." And then he went back along the same way and we remained sitting there. When night fell, we were ordered by the Serb soldiers who were standing guard around us to take our belongings and to move ahead in front of their soldiers. Those who were sitting outside the house stood up first, and they then went in the direction of Bratunac, across the fields. Those of us who were inside the house followed them, and we covered about 200 meters and after that we turned right, to the right, and went along the road leading from Potocari to Bratunac. We got to the road leading to the battery factory, which was in the vicinity of the UNPROFOR base, and two buses stood parked there. And the men who arrived first boarded the last bus, and those who came afterwards boarded the first bus. I got on the first bus, and at that time it was already crowded, and I could see on the right-hand side, on the right side of the bus, I could see General Mladic and several other soldiers around him. When I got on the bus, I saw a red car ahead of the bus, and after everybody had got on the bus, a Serb soldier entered the bus and he went to the driver. And he was standing there and carrying an automatic rifle. General Mladic approached the bus and he told the driver to shut the door and to follow the red car. The driver shut the door of the bus, and the red car set off and we followed it. And this is how we reached Bratunac. After that we went in the direction of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for a minute, Witness N. How many men were in the bus along with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: As many as they could put on the bus, because we were being told to move backwards to the bus, and this is how we got in. We were all cramped in that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a guard on the bus that accompanied you in the direction of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. There was a soldier who was armed with an automatic rifle. It was a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember how that soldier was dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: In camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What colour was the camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Green and dark green.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, where did you go in that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: We went to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you know -- did you stop in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you recognise the location where you had stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I recognised the location after we had passed by a school building. After that we stopped in front of an abandoned warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened when you stopped in front of that abandoned warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: We found a group of Serb soldiers there, and one of them approached the bus, the driver opened the door of the bus, and he ordered us out of the bus and he told us to march in front of the Serb soldiers. They had made a column, and we were marching in front of them, and this is how we entered the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many Serb soldiers were waiting for the arrival of your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to how those soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour, or were you able to distinguish the colour of those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Again, green and dark green camouflage uniforms. This is how we called them: camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you and did all of the men who were on the bus in which you travelled get off the bus and go into the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what did you do when you got inside the warehouse building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: We sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of a room was it that you sat down in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: It was off-white in colour. It had not been properly maintained, that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate dimensions of the room where you and the other men sat down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I think that it was about 15 meters long and 7 to 8 meters wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you and the men from your bus entered that room in the warehouse, did other Muslim men continue to arrive and fill the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe eventually how full that room was with Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: After the last group had been brought in, we were ordered to stand up and to move to the back, so that the last group who was outside could also get in. So we moved to the back as far as we could, and then the last group entered the warehouse and then we were ordered to sit down. But there was no longer enough room for everyone to sit down, so somebody -- some people sat down and others sat on their laps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, do you remember approximately what time of the evening it was when you arrived at this particular warehouse on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: It could have been about 10.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Judges your experiences that you had and what you observed happening to the other Muslim men who were in that room that particular night and the early morning hours that followed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: When we entered, there wasn't enough room, and we complained that we would suffocate. And then the Serb soldiers shot over our heads and shouted, "Keep silent or we'll kill you all," and then we fell silent. Then someone in the area where we had entered said, "You 12 have to carry out the assignment given to you. Do you understand that?" And he was speaking in a sharp tone. And then a group said, "Yes, sir," as one. And then Serb soldiers came with flashlights and they lighted us up. And then they asked where people were from, the people from Glogova, people from Cerska, people from Bratunac, and people answered. And then they said, "The people from Glogova get up." One man got up. The Serb soldiers said, "Come out here." He left the warehouse to the left, the direction through which we had entered the warehouse. We could hear blunt blows and his screams and moans. When all this stopped, again they came back with their flashlights, calling out people from various places. Nobody admitted to being from those places, so then the flashlight was pointed at anyone at random, and that person had to get up and go out. That is how they continued to kill people. Sometimes they would bring somebody back, badly beaten up, carrying them by the arms. They brought them to the doorway, and then a third one would push him into the room, and then the people were carrying -- that would carry this person from one hand to another. And this went on until the morning. In the morning they stopped taking people out. The people holding the dead complained that they couldn't stand it any longer, and they wanted to have them carried out. And so they allowed it and they let the people take out the dead bodies. Two people would take out the body and carry it outside the hall, behind the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you right there and ask you some questions, some additional questions about that particular night in the early morning hours. Were you able to hear the soldiers who were guarding you talk amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I was. They introduced themselves. They asked us, "Do you know who we are, whose soldiers we are?" We kept quiet; we didn't reply. And then they would hit each other on the soldier and say, "This one is an Arkanovac," and he would say yes. And then another one would say he belonged to the wolves, Drina Wolves, and he would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, during the night, in the early morning hours of the following morning, were you given any food? Were you given any water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: When they carried out the dead, we heard two trucks approaching the warehouse. We thought that they would be transporting us somewhere; however, a Serb soldier came to the doorway and said, "I need 10 volunteers, hard-working ones and younger ones, to do something for us." We knew immediately that they would be loading the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness N, let me just ask you to answer the question that I ask, and that is: Did you receive any water or did you receive any food the night of the 12th and the morning hours of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: We didn't receive anything until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you, and you were telling us about ten men who had been taken out. Would you please continue with your observations and what you recall about that incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Then they picked ten men, pointing them out with their fingers. Ten of them went out. There was silence for a while. While we could hear those motor vehicles departing from the warehouse, these ten men of ours never reappeared amongst us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were toilet facilities available to you and the other men who were being detained in the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Then they allowed us to go to the toilet and they showed us, as you go out of the warehouse, on the right-hand side, there was a room to be used as a toilet. So we went out, and I went out too. As I was coming from the toilet, I saw them taking one out of the line of men and taking him to the left. I saw two men standing on the left-hand side. There were Serb soldiers, two on the left, three on the right, and there was one facing the warehouse with an automatic rifle in his hand and shouting, "Come to me." And as he went toward him, he had stopped for a while, and this one kept saying, "Come here." And then on the left hand, the soldier standing to the left hit him with an iron rod on the head. And the Serb soldier standing on the right had a hatchet, and hit him on the back with the blade of the hatchet. I entered the big room, but they continued taking men out and killing them. And this went on until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you say "they took men out" and continued killing them, to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Serb soldiers. I mean Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they dressed in the same fashion that you've described earlier or were they dressed in a different fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: They were dressed in the same fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what time in the afternoon of the 13th did the killing stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: About 4.00 in the afternoon, about 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Then, again, we heard two motor vehicles approaching the warehouse. Again, one of the Serb soldiers asked for ten men to go out to do something for them. Nobody volunteered, so he selected ten men, who went out. There was silence for a while, and then again we heard the engines being turned on and the vehicles going away. Those ten men never returned to the warehouse either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened then, Witness N?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Then they stopped killing and they said General Mladic is coming now. And he appeared in the doorway, a general of the Serb army, Ratko Mladic. We asked him, "Why are you keeping us here? Why are you choking us here? Why don't you take us some place?" He said, "I haven't managed to negotiate your exchange earlier. We have agreed now, and you will all be exchanged and you're going to Kalesija to be exchanged. But let one of your men count how many you are so that I can determine how many buses I need." One of our men got up, and when he counted us, he said to Ratko Mladic that there were 296 of us. He said, "Sit down and vehicles will be coming to transport you to Kalesija."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now there were 296 men reported to be in the room, in the warehouse where you were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there other Muslim men located in other parts of the warehouse, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: When they came back, those of them who had taken the dead out of the warehouse, they came back in tears. We asked them, "What's wrong?" And they said, "It's not only that they're killing here, but they're killing somewhere else. They're bringing our men; our men are bringing them and putting them on the same pile." I heard this from the man who had taken out the dead bodies from our warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say the men who had taken out the dead bodies from your warehouse room, you're talking about the five dead Muslims who had been --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the five dead Muslims that ten of our men carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so what is your conclusion, Witness N, based on the conversations that you had with the men who had taken out the dead and returned? Is it your conclusion that there were other Muslim men being detained in the same warehouse but at different parts of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: That was our conclusion, that somewhere in the immediate vicinity there must have been other Muslim men that were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
